root_cause: Segment._split_cells guesses a starting char index with pos = int((cut / cell_length) * (len(text) - 1)) and then only scans FORWARD. With mixed-width text (CJK double-width + ASCII), the proportional guess can already be past the cut (cell_len(text[:pos]) > cut). The forward loop then adds one more char and takes the 'cell_pos > cut' branch, returning a left segment that is too wide. Example: '早乙女リリエル (CV: 徳井青）' split at 7 gives a 9-cell left part. Simulated on the base code, cuts 7, 9, 11, 13 and 14 are wrong, and the gold code gets every cut right.
best_solution: Make the starting guess never overshoot, so the forward-only scan can reach the cut. Gold changes it to pos = int((cut / cell_length) * len(text)) - 1, clamped to 0, and adds a docstring. The scan then moves forward from below the cut: it returns on an exact hit, or turns a straddled double-width char into two spaces. Starting at pos = 0 with cell_pos = 0 (a plain linear scan) is always correct, and a two-way adjust loop (what later rich versions use) also works. You can work this out from the statement alone. The linked Textual issue is about CJK text, so test the invariant cell_len(left) == cut for every cut on a long mixed-width string. The bug shows up at once, and the one-directional scan after a proportional estimate is the defect.
acceptable_alternatives: Start the scan at pos = 0 / cell_pos = 0 (v6/v7 did this and passed). Rewrite as a clean linear accumulate loop that splits a straddled wide char into two spaces (v4 did this and passed). Or keep the estimate and add a backward step while cell_len(text[:pos]) > cut. Any O(n) scan passes, because the tests only check correctness.
hidden_test_demands: tests/test_segment.py adds test_split_cells_mixed ('早乙女リリエル (CV: 徳井青）'), test_split_cells_doubles ('早'*20) and test_split_cells_single ('A'*20). For every position in 1..cell_length-1 each one asserts cell_len(left.text) == position and cell_len(right.text) == cell_length - position. A straddled double-width char must become ' ' + ' ' so the widths still add up. No new API or exact strings.
locating_signals: The statement names the function exactly: 'Segment._split_cells'. The only other signal is the link to textual#4996, whose text (CJK text rendering wrong) the agent cannot see. The location is trivial to find; the hard part is finding which input fails, because short emoji-only strings work on the base code.
our_outcome_summary: v4, v6 and v7 PASSED; v8 FAILED. v4 rewrote the function as a linear scan from 0 (38s, 12 calls). v6 and v7 replaced the proportional guess with pos=0/cell_pos=0 (30s and 72s). v8 (117s, 26 calls) made no functional change: it only added a comment after a return statement. Its repro probes used single or double emoji and short strings like 'A🍎', where the base code is correct. It concluded the two-spaces behavior was intended and 'fixed' the task with a comment. Its own verifier test used the same easy inputs, so it passed. Hidden test failure: test_split_cells_mixed, assert 9 == 7.
generalizable_lesson: For a terse 'fix <function>' statement with an unreadable issue link, check the function's contract as an invariant over the whole input space (every cut position, every index) on adversarial inputs: mixed-width or unicode text, long strings, boundaries. Hand-picking a few easy cases can miss the bug. Look for heuristic shortcuts such as a proportional estimate followed by a one-directional scan: they fail when the estimate lands on the wrong side. Never submit a comment-only or no-behavior-change patch for a bugfix task. If you cannot reproduce the bug, you have not found the failing input yet.
